page_hint: Ch 9, §5 Common Mistakes, first bullet, parenthetical
quoted_clause: by the ring model of §3 each link still carries (N−1)/N of the tensor
observed: The cross-reference uses '§3' (within-chapter shorthand) while every other reference to the same section in this chapter uses '§9.3' (e.g., 'the §9.3 worked example', 'The eight-rank ring in §9.3', '§9.4 measurements').
evidence: Search of Chapter 9 text: '§9.3' appears 4 times; '§3' appears 1 time (this instance). The chapter's own convention is the fully-qualified form.
root_cause: Inconsistent cross-reference style within a single chapter.
correction: Change '§3' to '§9.3' to match the chapter's established convention.
acceptance_test: All intra-chapter section references in Chapter 9 use the '§9.N' form; no bare '§N' remains.

page_hint: Ch 10, §3 Worked Example, Pipeline Parallelism subsection, paragraph after the speedup formula
quoted_clause: the P−1 term in the denominator is the bubble: the pipeline fills and drains exactly once per m-batch pass, so P−1 stage-slots are wasted out of the m·P slots each stage would otherwise work
observed: The phrase 'P−1 stage-slots are wasted out of the m·P slots' is slightly imprecise. The m·P quantity is the total useful work (m micro-batches × P stages), but the pipeline's total time is (m+P−1) stage-time units, not m·P. The P−1 extra time units are the bubble, but they are not 'wasted out of m·P slots'—they are added to the m useful time units to make m+P−1 total. A reader doing the arithmetic may be confused by the denominator framing.
evidence: For P=4, m=8: total time = 11 stage-units; useful work = 32 stage-units (8×4); bubble = 3 stage-units (P−1). The speedup is 32/11, not 32/(32−3). The 'P−1 out of m·P' framing conflates the time-domain bubble with the work-domain total.
root_cause: The explanation tries to give intuition for the denominator (m+P−1) by referencing the numerator (mP), but the 'wasted out of' phrasing implies a subtraction from mP rather than an addition to m.
correction: Rephrase to: 'the pipeline takes m+P−1 stage-time units to complete m·P units of useful work; the P−1 extra units are the fill-and-drain bubble. The ideal speedup over a single serial pass (m·P units) is therefore mP/(m+P−1).'
acceptance_test: A reader can verify the P=4, m=8 case: 11 time units for 32 useful units → speedup 32/11 ≈ 2.9, without needing to reconcile 'P−1 out of m·P' with the actual denominator.

page_hint: Ch 10, §7 What We Still Don't Know, second bullet (MoE scaling)
quoted_clause: Kimi K3 activates just 16 of 896 routed experts per token (2.8T total / 104B active) via its Stable LatentMoE
observed: A reader doing the arithmetic gets 16/896 × 2.8T ≈ 50B, not 104B. The discrepancy is because 'active parameters' in MoE literature includes non-expert components (attention, shared layers, embeddings), but the text does not state this. The subsequent sentence '16/896 ≈ 1.8% expert activation' correctly refers to the expert routing fraction, but the juxtaposition with '104B active' without explanation invites confusion.
evidence: 16 × (2.8T / 896) = 16 × 3.125B = 50B (expert-only active). 104B − 50B = 54B (non-expert active: attention, shared FFN, embeddings, etc.). The text does not decompose this.
root_cause: The parenthetical '(2.8T total / 104B active)' uses the standard MoE 'active parameters' convention without flagging that it includes non-expert components, creating an apparent arithmetic inconsistency with the 16/896 routing ratio.
correction: Add a brief clause: '(2.8T total; 104B active, of which ~50B is the 16 routed experts and the remainder is attention and shared layers)'. Alternatively, rephrase to: 'activates 16 of 896 routed experts per token (≈1.8% expert activation; 2.8T total parameters, 104B active including non-expert components)'.
acceptance_test: A reader who computes 16/896 × 2.8T does not encounter an unexplained gap between the result (~50B) and the stated 'active' figure (104B).

page_hint: Ch 9, §5 Common Mistakes, first bullet, final sentence
quoted_clause: Measured effective bandwidth is typically 40–60% of peak [ILLUSTRATIVE]; design against the measured number, not the spec sheet peak.
observed: The 40–60% range is reasonable for the specific context described (multi-GPU, multi-link, moderate-to-large messages), but as stated it reads as a universal planning constant. For small messages (latency-dominated), effective bandwidth can be well below 40% of peak; for very large messages on a well-tuned single-rail path, it can approach 80–90%. The [ILLUSTRATIVE] tag helps, but the sentence structure ('typically 40–60%') presents it as a general rule.
evidence: The preceding sentence scopes the context: 'in multi-GPU topologies the traffic is split across multiple GPUs and multiple links, so one link rarely carries the whole transfer.' The 40–60% is appropriate for that context but the sentence does not explicitly bind the range to it.
root_cause: The planning heuristic is stated as a general 'typically' rather than as a context-specific range.
correction: Tighten the scope: 'For the multi-link, multi-GPU case described above, measured effective bandwidth is often in the 40–60% range of the per-link peak [ILLUSTRATIVE]; for small messages the ratio is lower (latency-dominated), and for a single large transfer on one well-configured link it can be higher. Design against the measured number for your specific message size and topology, not the spec sheet peak.'
acceptance_test: A reader does not apply '40–60%' to a 64-byte all-reduce or to a single 140 GB transfer on one NVLink without questioning whether the range applies.

page_hint: Ch 11, §3 Worked Example, 'When to Disaggregate' subsection, first sentence of the P/D paragraph
quoted_clause: prefill is compute-bound (~1.29 PFLOP → ~1.19 PFLOPS required over the ~1.08 s prefill budget, vs 0.989 PFLOPS peak), decode is bandwidth-bound (the whole-model weight-read rate of ~5.6 TB/s if served by one device vs 3.35 TB/s per GPU
observed: The prefill figure (1.19 PFLOPS required vs 0.989 PFLOPS peak) shows a single H100 cannot meet the prefill budget, which is correct. However, the text does not explicitly state the consequence: that the 8×H100 host (7.912 PFLOPS aggregate) has ~6.6× headroom for prefill, and the binding constraint for prefill on the canonical host is not raw FLOPS but the scheduling/batching interaction with decode. As written, a reader might conclude that prefill is 'infeasible' on a single H100 (true) but miss that the 8-GPU host is comfortably in the compute-bound regime for prefill and the real P/D tension is the scheduling conflict, not a raw capacity shortfall.
evidence: 8 × 0.989 = 7.912 PFLOPS aggregate. Required: 1.19 PFLOPS. Ratio: 6.6×. The text states the per-device numbers but does not close the loop to the 8-device host that is the canonical baseline.
root_cause: The per-device comparison is correct but the architectural consequence for the canonical 8×H100 host is left implicit, weakening the 'why disaggregate' argument at the scale where it actually matters (multi-node, not single-host).
correction: After the per-device numbers, add one sentence: 'On the canonical 8×H100 host the aggregate prefill capacity (≈7.9 PFLOPS) exceeds the 1.19 PFLOPS requirement by a wide margin; the P/D tension on a single host is a scheduling conflict (batching for prefill inflates decode latency), not a raw FLOPS shortfall. The raw-capacity argument becomes binding only when the workload outgrows one node and the two phases must be placed on separate, independently sized pools.'
acceptance_test: A reader can distinguish (a) the single-GPU infeasibility that motivates TP, from (b) the scheduling conflict that motivates P/D on a single host, from (c) the independent-sizing benefit that motivates P/D at multi-node scale.

page_hint: Ch 9, §5 Common Mistakes, fifth bullet (protocol overhead)
quoted_clause: An NDR 400 Gb/s InfiniBand link delivers a ~380 Gb/s class useful payload; a 200 Gb/s RoCE2 link delivers ~180 Gb/s. The difference matters when we are computing per-second throughput for a fixed data volume.
observed: The two figures compare different nominal link speeds (400 vs 200 Gb/s), which makes the 'difference' partly a speed difference and partly an overhead difference. The intended point—that protocol overhead reduces useful payload below the nominal rate, and that the reduction differs between IB and RoCE2—is valid but obscured by the mismatched baselines. A reader may focus on the 380 vs 180 ratio (≈2.1×) and miss that the nominal ratio is 2× (400/200), so the overhead effect is only ~5% additional.
evidence: 400 × 64/66 ≈ 388 Gb/s (IB line-coding); minus IB headers → ~380. 200 × 64/66 ≈ 194 Gb/s (RoCE2 line-coding); minus Ethernet + RoCE headers → ~180. The overhead fractions are ~3% (IB) and ~7% (RoCE2). The 2.1× vs 2× difference is small.
root_cause: The example uses different link speeds, making the overhead comparison less direct than intended.
correction: Either (a) compare at the same nominal speed: 'A 200 Gb/s InfiniBand HDR link delivers ~190 Gb/s useful payload; a 200 Gb/s RoCE2 link delivers ~180 Gb/s. The ~5% gap matters when computing per-second throughput for a fixed data volume.' Or (b) keep the 400/200 comparison but add: 'At the same nominal speed the gap is smaller (~3% for IB vs ~7% for RoCE2), but it compounds over the 2× speed difference, so the 380/180 ≈ 2.1× ratio slightly exceeds the nominal 2×.'
acceptance_test: A reader can isolate the protocol-overhead effect from the nominal-speed effect and understand the magnitude of each.

page_hint: Ch 12, Table 12-2, rows 'Prefill hosts, avg 92K tok/s' and 'Prefill hosts, peak 368K tok/s', column (c)
quoted_clause: Prefill hosts, avg 92K tok/s | ~5 | prefill pool ~5 | ~4 (92,000 ÷ 24,725 ≈ 3.72)
observed: The column header is 'Prefill hosts' but for candidate (c) the divisor 24,725 is the per-GPU (single H100) prefill rate, not the per-host (8×H100) rate of 197,800. The ~4 and ~15 are therefore counts of individual H100 cards, not 8×H100 hosts. A reader who reads only the table (without the footnote below it) would interpret '~4 hosts' as 4 × 8×H100 = 32 H100s, a factor-of-8 overestimate of the actual requirement.
evidence: 24,725 tok/s is explicitly the single-GPU rate (989 TFLOP/s × 0.35 / 14 GFLOP). The 8-GPU node rate is 8 × 24,725 = 197,800 tok/s, which the footnote below the table confirms is 'not this layout.' 92,000 / 24,725 = 3.72 → 4 cards; 368,000 / 24,725 = 14.88 → 15 cards. If these were 8×H100 hosts, the correct figures would be 92,000 / 197,800 = 0.47 → 1 host and 368,000 / 197,800 = 1.86 → 2 hosts.
root_cause: The table uses a single column header ('Prefill hosts') for three candidates with different hardware units (8×H100 hosts for a/b, single H100 cards for c). The footnote below the table corrects the interpretation, but the table itself is misleading when read in isolation.
correction: Either (a) change the column header to 'Prefill units (hosts for a/b; H100 cards for c)' and annotate the (c) cells as '~4 H100 cards' and '~15 H100 cards'; or (b) add a per-candidate unit row above the data rows: '(a)/(b): 8×H100 hosts; (c): single H100 cards'; or (c) convert (c) to host-equivalents: 4 cards = 0.5 host, 15 cards = 1.9 hosts, with a note that (c) does not use 8-GPU nodes.
acceptance_test: A reader who sees only Table 12-2 (without the footnote) can correctly identify the hardware unit for each candidate's prefill count.

page_hint: Ch 12, §12.2 Mental Model, first paragraph, resource list
quoted_clause: compute (prefill throughput — prefill is compute-bound, Ch 11), memory bandwidth (decode throughput — decode is bandwidth-bound)
observed: The phrases 'prefill is compute-bound' and 'decode is bandwidth-bound' are stated as unqualified universal properties. The review standard requires these to be presented as first-order regimes whose validity depends on model architecture, sequence length, batch size, precision, kernels, and hardware. The 'Ch 11' reference provides a path to the full qualification, but a reader who skips Ch 11 (or reads this chapter out of order) takes the statements as laws.
evidence: Prefill can be bandwidth-bound at very short sequences (where the weight-read dominates over the FLOPs) or with aggressive quantization (where the FLOP count drops but the weight bytes remain). Decode can be compute-bound at very large batch sizes (where the attention FLOPs grow with batch²) or with FlashAttention-style kernels that change the arithmetic intensity. The canonical 70B/9.2K/8×H100 operating point is where the stated regimes hold.
root_cause: Shorthand in a resource list omits the operating-point qualifier that the full analysis in Ch 11 provides.
correction: Add a brief qualifier: 'compute (prefill throughput — at the canonical operating point, prefill is compute-bound; Ch 11 gives the full regime analysis), memory bandwidth (decode throughput — at the canonical operating point, decode is bandwidth-bound; Ch 11).' Alternatively, add a single sentence after the list: 'These regime labels hold for the canonical 70B / 9.2K / 8×H100 configuration; the boundary conditions are analyzed in Ch 11.'
acceptance_test: A reader who encounters this sentence without having read Ch 11 does not conclude that prefill is universally compute-bound regardless of sequence length, batch size, or precision.

page_hint: Ch 13, §13.1 Concept, item 3 (Cluster tier definition)
quoted_clause: Required when a model exceeds a node's memory (so it must be split per Ch10) or when traffic outgrows one host (so P/D disaggregation per Ch11 applies).
observed: The cluster-tier definition states that traffic outgrowing one host leads to 'P/D disaggregation per Ch11.' But the 10× traffic worked example in §13.3 responds to traffic growth with data parallelism (replication: 'run N identical 8×H100 hosts behind a load balancer'), not P/D disaggregation. P/D disaggregation is one possible response to traffic, but simple DP is the more common and simpler first response. The tier definition over-specifies the mechanism.
evidence: §13.3: 'Response: replicate the model across multiple servers (data parallelism at the serving layer — run N identical 8×H100 hosts behind a load balancer).' The 10× example never invokes P/D disaggregation. P/D disaggregation appears in Ch 11 and Ch 12 as a separate optimization, not as the default traffic response.
root_cause: The tier definition was written with P/D disaggregation as the canonical traffic response, but the worked example uses the simpler DP response. The definition should enumerate the options, not prescribe one.
correction: Change to: 'Required when a model exceeds a node's memory (so it must be split per Ch10) or when traffic outgrows one host (requiring multi-host scaling: data-parallel replication, P/D disaggregation, or both — Ch 11/17).'
acceptance_test: The tier definition is consistent with the 10× worked example, which uses DP replication, and does not imply that P/D disaggregation is the only or default response to traffic growth.

page_hint: Ch 11, §11.6 Architecture Consequence, first bullet (Baseline)
quoted_clause: PagedAttention ensures the ~24.1 GB-per-request KV pack fits
observed: PagedAttention does not 'ensure' the KV pack fits. The KV pack fitting is a memory-capacity question (does 24.1 GB × N concurrent requests fit in the available HBM?). PagedAttention is a memory-management strategy that reduces fragmentation so that the available HBM can be efficiently allocated to concurrent requests. Without PagedAttention, the 24.1 GB per request might still fit, but fragmentation would waste a larger fraction of the available memory, reducing the number of concurrent requests that can be served.
evidence: The book's own terminology (Ch 11, §11.6, Fig 11.2) defines state management as 'PagedAttention (fixed-size KV pages)' and describes it as managing 'how KV is allocated/fragmented.' The capacity question (does it fit?) is separate from the allocation question (can the available memory be used without fragmentation waste?).
root_cause: The word 'ensures' conflates the capacity constraint (total HBM ≥ total KV) with the allocation efficiency (fragmentation overhead).
correction: Change to: 'PagedAttention manages the KV allocation so that the ~24.1 GB per request can be packed into the available HBM with minimal fragmentation overhead.' Or: 'PagedAttention ensures that the available HBM is efficiently allocated to the ~24.1 GB-per-request KV packs (minimizing fragmentation waste).'
acceptance_test: The sentence distinguishes between the memory-capacity constraint (does the KV fit?) and the allocation-efficiency role of PagedAttention (can the available memory be used without fragmentation waste?).

page_hint: Ch 11, Fig 11.3 caption and Note 11.3-1
quoted_clause: it moves the per-request KV state (~35 GB, §9.8) across the joining link
observed: The ~35 GB per-request KV corresponds to 13.3K tokens (35 / 2.62 ≈ 13.3K), not the canonical 9.2K tokens (which gives 24.1 GB) or 9.5K (24.9 GB). The Note 11.3-1 explains the derivation ('13.3K = 35 GB ÷ 2.62 MB, the count ch 9 quotes'), but the main caption presents '~35 GB' as 'the per-request KV state' without flagging that this is a different context length than the canonical workload the reader has been working with. A reader expecting 24.1 GB (canonical 9.2K) encounters 35 GB without an in-caption explanation.
evidence: Canonical: 9,200 × 2.62 = 24,104 MB ≈ 24.1 GB. Figure: 13,300 × 2.62 = 34,846 MB ≈ 35 GB. The 13.3K figure is attributed to §9.8, which presumably uses a different (larger) context for its analysis. The figure is about P/D disaggregation in general, not specifically the canonical workload, so a different context is defensible, but the transition is not signposted in the caption.
root_cause: The figure uses a non-canonical context length (13.3K from Ch 9) without explicitly noting the difference from the canonical 9.2K in the caption.
correction: In the main caption, change 'the per-request KV state (~35 GB, §9.8)' to 'the per-request KV state (~35 GB at the 13.3K-token context used in §9.8; the canonical 9.2K context gives ~24.1 GB).' This one clause prevents the reader from confusing the two figures.
acceptance_test: A reader who has been working with the canonical 9.2K / 24.1 GB figures can immediately identify why the figure shows 35 GB and not 24.1 GB, without needing to read the full Note 11.3-1.

page_hint: Ch 12, §12.3 Worked Example, Candidate (b) paragraph
quoted_clause: Each pool therefore needs its own 8×H100 host (residency = 140 GB weights plus the pool's in-flight KV population — at the canonical per-host KV budget (640 − 140 weights − ~64 runtime ≈ 436 GB, Ch 7/17), ~140 + ~436 = ~576 GB — comfortably under 640 GB; one request's 24 GB is not the pool's population).
observed: The 576 GB figure (140 + 436) is presented as the residency for 'each pool,' but the two pools have fundamentally different KV profiles. The decode pool holds accumulated KV for all in-flight generation requests (up to the full 436 GB budget). The prefill pool creates KV transiently during prefill and immediately transfers it to the decode pool; its steady-state KV occupancy is the KV for requests currently being prefilled (a small fraction of 436 GB). Stating 576 GB for 'each pool' overestimates the prefill pool's actual memory usage and obscures an important architectural asymmetry.
evidence: In P/D disaggregation, the prefill pool's KV is created and transferred within the prefill duration (~1.08 s for the canonical 9.2K input). The decode pool's KV persists for the full generation duration (~7.5 s for 300 output tokens at 40 tok/s). The prefill pool's concurrent KV population is proportional to the prefill rate × prefill duration, not the total in-flight population. The 436 GB budget is the maximum possible KV for either pool, but the prefill pool's actual usage is much lower in steady state.
root_cause: The text uses a single worst-case upper bound (436 GB) for both pools without distinguishing the prefill pool's transient KV from the decode pool's persistent KV.
correction: Add a sentence after the 576 GB figure: 'Note the asymmetry: the decode pool's KV is persistent (accumulated over the full generation), so it approaches the 436 GB budget under load; the prefill pool's KV is transient (created and transferred within the ~1.1 s prefill), so its steady-state KV occupancy is a small fraction of 436 GB. The 576 GB figure is the worst-case upper bound that applies to the decode pool; the prefill pool's actual residency is lower.'
acceptance_test: A reader understands that the two pools have different KV memory profiles and that the 576 GB figure is a worst-case bound for the decode pool, not a typical value for both pools.

page_hint: Ch 12, §12.3, Candidate (a), throughput gate paragraph
quoted_clause: the gate closes only when the host class is replicated to ~5 hosts on the average prefill screen (92K ÷ 19.8K ≈ 4.65 → 5), ~6 on the average KV/service-time screen (10 × 8.6 ÷ 17 ≈ 5.06 → 6), and ~21 at peak (40 × 8.6 ÷ 17 ≈ 20.2 → 21)
observed: The sentence lists three host counts (5, 6, 21) for the 'throughput at the SLO' gate without explicitly stating that the gate requires ALL sub-constraints to be met simultaneously, so the binding constraint is the maximum. At average load, the binding constraint is the KV/service-time screen (6 hosts, not 5). At peak, it is 21. A reader might interpret the list as three alternative thresholds rather than three concurrent constraints whose maximum governs.
evidence: The three sub-constraints are: (1) prefill compute: 92K / 19.8K = 4.65 → 5 hosts; (2) KV residency: 10 × 8.6 / 17 = 5.06 → 6 hosts; (3) peak KV residency: 40 × 8.6 / 17 = 20.2 → 21 hosts. The gate passes only when all three are satisfied, so the minimum host count is max(5, 6) = 6 at average and 21 at peak. The text does not state this 'take the maximum' rule explicitly.
root_cause: The three sub-constraints are listed in parallel without an explicit 'all must hold; the binding one is the maximum' statement.
correction: Add a clarifying clause: 'The gate requires all three sub-constraints to hold simultaneously; the binding constraint is the maximum. At average load, the KV/service-time screen (6 hosts) binds, not the prefill screen (5). At peak, the KV/service-time screen (21 hosts) binds.'
acceptance_test: A reader can identify which sub-constraint is binding at each load level without re-deriving the maximum.

page_hint: Ch 13, §13.3, 'Escalating: When 10×Traffic Forces the Cluster Tier', first bullet
quoted_clause: continuous batching on 8×H100 at ~9.5K tokens/request sustained roughly tens of thousands of tokens/s; goodput against the SLO is the binding number.
observed: The phrase 'roughly tens of thousands of tokens/s' is vague when a specific, previously established number is available: 19,800 prefill tokens/s per 8×H100 host at 35% MFU (Ch 8, used throughout Ch 12). The reader has just seen this number in Ch 12's candidate analysis. Using a vague approximation here weakens the argument and forces the reader to reconstruct the specific figure.
evidence: Ch 12, §12.3, Candidate (a): 'a single 8×H100 host sustains only ~19,800 prefill-tokens/s at the idealized 35%-MFU aggregate (8 × 2,472; see the Ch. 8 scope note).' This is the same hardware and model. The 10× scenario's 950K tokens/s demand is ~48× the 19,800 prefill rate, a much more striking ratio than 'tens of thousands.'
root_cause: The 10× escalation paragraph was written as a standalone illustration and did not cross-reference the specific Ch 8/Ch 12 figure.
correction: Replace 'sustained roughly tens of thousands of tokens/s' with 'sustains ~19,800 prefill tokens/s (Ch 8, 35% MFU; the same figure used in Ch 12's candidate analysis).' Then the comparison '950K / 19.8K ≈ 48×' makes the magnitude of the gap explicit.
acceptance_test: The 10× escalation paragraph contains a specific, traceable throughput figure rather than a vague approximation, and the reader can compute the demand-to-capacity ratio directly.

page_hint: Ch 13, §13.3, 10× escalation paragraph, the sentence beginning 'At ~100 rps average, the book's whole-slot KV/service-time screen...'
quoted_clause: the ~2.0 rps screen uses the unfloored 17.5-slot quotient and applies no utilization headroom, so 50 hosts could only deliver 50 × 17/8.6 ≈ 98.8 rps — below demand.
observed: The sentence says the screen 'uses the unfloored 17.5-slot quotient' but then calculates '50 × 17/8.6' using the floored 17. The 2.0 rps figure comes from 17.5/8.6 ≈ 2.03 (rounded to 2.0), but the actual per-host delivery rate is 17/8.6 = 1.977. The text mixes the two quotients in one sentence without explaining why the analytical 17.5 is used to derive the 2.0 rps but the provisioning 17 is used to compute the actual delivery. A reader following the arithmetic will see 17.5 in one clause and 17 in the next and be confused.
evidence: 17.5 / 8.6 = 2.035 ≈ 2.0 (analytical, unfloored). 17 / 8.6 = 1.977 (provisioning, floored). 50 × 2.035 = 101.7 rps (if using 17.5). 50 × 1.977 = 98.8 rps (if using 17). The text uses 17.5 to get 2.0, then 17 to get 98.8, without flagging the switch.
root_cause: The explanation of why the naive 50-host calculation understates the fleet mixes the analytical (17.5) and provisioning (17) quotients in a single sentence.
correction: Rewrite as: 'The naive 100 / 2.0 ≈ 50 uses the rounded analytical rate (17.5 / 8.6 ≈ 2.03, rounded to 2.0). But the actual per-host delivery rate uses the floored provisioning quotient: 17 / 8.6 = 1.977 rps. So 50 hosts deliver 50 × 1.977 ≈ 98.8 rps — below the 100 rps demand. The ~1.2 rps gap is the cost of the 17.5 → 17 floor.'
acceptance_test: A reader can trace the 17.5 → 2.0 → 50 chain and the 17 → 1.977 → 98.8 chain separately, and understand why they differ.

page_hint: Ch 12, §12.8 Mini-Case, economic ceiling paragraph
quoted_clause: the economic constraint, as stated, fails at fleet scale. Economics is therefore recorded as *not yet passed (deferred)*, and the architect's first return-to-synthesis move is to renegotiate the budget, shape peak demand, or revisit the model class.
observed: The text earlier states that the economic ceiling 'is not one of the three gates' (§12.1). But here it 'fails' and is 'recorded as not yet passed (deferred),' using the same gate language ('passed', 'fails') as the three technical gates. This creates a category confusion: is the economic constraint a gate or not? The text's intent is that the economic constraint is a business viability check that forces a return to synthesis, not a technical feasibility gate that eliminates a candidate architecture. The language should distinguish these two types of failure.
evidence: §12.1: 'The economic ceiling is recorded but is not one of the three gates; §12.8 states its consequence at fleet scale.' §12.8: 'the economic constraint, as stated, fails at fleet scale. Economics is therefore recorded as *not yet passed (deferred)*.' The words 'fails' and 'not yet passed' are the same vocabulary used for the three gates (e.g., 'the throughput gate does not pass,' 'the quality gate is open').
root_cause: The economic constraint is discussed using gate vocabulary ('fails,' 'not yet passed') despite being explicitly excluded from the three gates.
correction: Change to: 'the economic constraint, as stated, is not met at fleet scale. This is not a gate failure (the three technical gates are unaffected) but a business-viability finding: the stated budget cannot cover the required fleet. The architect's first return-to-synthesis move is to renegotiate the budget, shape peak demand, or revisit the model class.'
acceptance_test: A reader can distinguish between a technical gate failure (eliminates a candidate architecture) and a business-viability finding (forces a return to synthesis to change the problem parameters) without confusion.

page_hint: Ch 11, §11.6, Fig 11.2 caption and the italicized 'design lever' sentence
quoted_clause: Serving is four separable concerns, not a stack (they interact — batching pressure feeds KV residency — but each is chosen independently)
observed: The main claim is that the four concerns are 'separable' and 'chosen independently,' but the parenthetical immediately acknowledges that 'they interact — batching pressure feeds KV residency.' If the choice of batching strategy (request scheduling) affects KV residency (state management), then the choices are not fully independent. The 'independently' claim is in tension with the acknowledged interaction. The four concerns have independent *primary design variables*, but the choices are coupled through shared resources.
evidence: The text itself provides the counterexample: 'batching pressure feeds KV residency.' A higher batching concurrency (request scheduling choice) increases the total KV in flight (state management constraint). The two are not independently choosable: the maximum concurrency is bounded by the KV budget, which is a state-management parameter.
root_cause: The 'independently' claim is too strong given the acknowledged interactions. The correct statement is that each concern has its own primary design variable, but the feasible region for each variable is constrained by the others.
correction: Change to: 'Serving is four separable concerns, not a stack. Each has its own primary design variable (batching policy, page size, cache key, pool split), and the variables can be chosen in any order. But they interact through shared resources — batching pressure feeds KV residency, and the KV budget in turn bounds the maximum concurrency — so the feasible region for each dial is shaped by the others.'
acceptance_test: A reader understands that the four concerns are designable in any order (separable) but that the choices are coupled through shared resources (not fully independent).

page_hint: Ch 12, 'The Architect's Question' section, last sentence
quoted_clause: This distinguishes our approach from the abstract meta-method presented in Ch. 22, which operates at a level of generality that does not instantiate against concrete substrate constraints.
observed: This is a forward reference to Ch 22 that the reader cannot resolve at this point. The phrase 'abstract meta-method' and 'level of generality that does not instantiate against concrete substrate constraints' are not enough for the reader to understand what Ch 22 does or why the distinction matters. The reader at Ch 12 has not seen Ch 22 and cannot evaluate the contrast.

page_hint: Ch 11, §11.6, diffusion model paragraph, FDFO sentence
quoted_clause: The SGLang diffusion scheduler inspected on 2026-10-28 (revision a1966e1) implements a first-done-first-out path that retains partial block state.

The reader needs to understand what FDFO means in practice: requests that complete their current refinement round first are served next, rather than all requests in a batch waiting for the slowest member to complete the same round (lockstep). This is a meaningful scheduling distinction from the lockstep approach described in the preceding sentence, but the reader must infer it from the name.

The FDFO path is the 'unless' case, but the mechanism (which request is served next, what state is retained) is not explained.

This contrasts with lockstep, where all batch members must complete the same round before any advances.'

page_hint: Ch 14, §14.3, Step 2, paragraph after the sweep description
quoted_clause: The scenario's 40 req/s peak and assumed 8.6-second execution time imply about 344 executing requests fleet-wide, not resident requests on one host.
observed: The sentence correctly distinguishes fleet-wide executing requests (344) from per-host resident requests (17), but the phrase 'executing requests' is ambiguous. In queuing theory, 'executing' (or 'in service') means the request is being processed, not queued. The 344 figure (40 × 8.6) is the total number of requests in the system (executing + queued) at steady state under Little's Law, assuming no queueing (all 344 are simultaneously in service across the fleet). If there is queueing, the 344 includes queued requests. The text should clarify that 344 is the total in-system population under the no-queue assumption, or that it is the executing population when the fleet is sized to eliminate queueing.
evidence: Little's Law: L = λW, where L is the average number in the system, λ is the arrival rate, and W is the average time in the system. 40 × 8.6 = 344 is L (total in system). If the fleet has exactly 344/17 = 20.2 hosts (rounded to 21), and each host serves 17 concurrent requests, then 21 × 17 = 357 ≥ 344, so queueing is minimal. But the 344 is the in-system count, not strictly the 'executing' count unless queueing is zero.
root_cause: The term 'executing' is used where 'in the system' or 'in flight (executing or queued)' would be more precise.
correction: Change to: 'The scenario's 40 req/s peak and assumed 8.6-second execution time imply about 344 requests in the system fleet-wide (by Little's Law: 40 × 8.6), not 344 resident on one host. A single host holds at most 17 concurrent requests (the floored KV-residency quotient).'
acceptance_test: A reader understands that 344 is the total in-system population (executing + any queued) across the entire fleet, not the per-host resident count.
